content: Acrodynia is a condition that presents with a pink discoloration of the hands and feet, accompanied by irritability, sensitivity to light (photophobia), and inflammation of the nerves (polyneuritis). Initial Signs In the early stages, affected individuals may exhibit symptoms such as lethargy, excessive sleepiness, irritability, and a tendency to cry frequently. There is often a noticeable loss of appetite, which can lead to weight loss. More than half of the patients report sensitivity to light. Generalized weakness and pain in the extremities are also common. Symptoms Within 2-4 Weeks As the condition progresses, the tips of the nose, fingers, and toes develop a pinkish discoloration, which gradually darkens and spreads into a net-like pattern. The hands and feet become painful, cold, bluish (cyanotic), red (erythematous), and swollen. The affected extremities often experience severe pain and itching, prompting the child to rub or scratch the area, which can result in thickened, damaged skin. Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis) with a distinctive mouselike odor may occur, potentially leading to miliaria (sweat gland obstruction) and secondary bacterial skin infections. The gums may become inflamed, swollen, and eroded, which can result in tooth loss. Hair loss (alopecia) and nail loss have also been reported in some cases. Gastrointestinal System Symptoms include inflammation of the mouth (stomatitis) accompanied by loss of appetite (anorexia). Colitis may occur, leading to diarrhea or constipation. Excessive salivation is also a frequent finding. Renal System Proteinuria (the presence of protein in the urine) is a common renal symptom. In severe cases, nephrotic syndrome may develop, potentially progressing to renal failure. Skin The palms, soles, and face may exhibit redness (erythema). Swelling (edema) and peeling (desquamation) of the skin on the hands and feet are common. Intense itching (pruritus) is frequently reported. Muscular and Skeletal System Patients may experience reduced muscle tone (hypotonia). Miscellaneous Symptoms Other symptoms include gum inflammation (gingivitis), excessive sweating (diaphoresis), abnormal sensations such as tingling or numbness (paresthesia), and generalized pain throughout the body. Treatment The primary goal of treatment is to eliminate mercury from the body and address any fluid or electrolyte imbalances. Chelating agents, such as meso-2,3-dimercaptosuccinic acid, are used to prevent the uptake of methylmercury by red blood cells and liver cells. In cases of acute renal failure caused by mercury toxicity, hemodialysis may be employed, with or without the addition of L-cysteine as a chelating agent.
